requirements-specification.md §13.2 AS-34 (Basis) and AS-35; research-report.md §9 (fifth bullet) — the protection estimate for the overall cap of 20 assumes PINs are chosen at random, which overstates the protection more than tenfold — AS-34 says "If the PIN is 4 digits chosen at random, 20 guesses find it 0.2% of the time". Members' PINs are not random. A peer-reviewed study of user-chosen PINs (Markert, Golla, Dürmuth, Bailey and Aviv, 2020; arXiv 2003.04868, Table VI) found that an attacker limited to a few guesses finds 5% of 4-digit PINs in 10 guesses and 8% in 30. It also found 6-digit PINs add little. A 2012 DataGenetics analysis of 3.4 million leaked PINs, as reported by Schneier, found the 20 most common make up 26.8% of them. Some UK library systems set the PIN to the member's date of birth: UCL Library says "Your PIN is four digits and for UCL students is set automatically to your date of birth (Day/Day/Month/Month)", which leaves 366 possible values. AS-35 and §9 also say the PIN's length "sets how much protection the cap gives", but the evidence shows how PINs are chosen matters more. Council IT is asked to validate the cap of 20 on this basis.
uplift: (1) In AS-34, replace the 0.2% sentence with an evidence-based one. Add Markert et al. (2020) to the source register as peer-reviewed and labelled "older; foundational", then write: "for member-chosen 4-digit PINs, 20 guesses would succeed for roughly 5–8% of cards (**estimate**, between the study's 10- and 30-guess figures [S#]); 0.2% applies only if PINs were random". (2) Extend AS-35 and research §9 to ask how PINs are set (chosen by the member, a default such as date of birth, or any block on common PINs) as well as their length. (3) Say that council IT should weigh this when validating 20, and that NIST allows any lower cap [S76].

research-report.md §5.5 F-34 (the NIST bullet), §7 (the NIST row), §8 R-14, §9, §10 C-18 ("meets it"); requirements-specification.md §10 NFR-26 rationale ("20 meets both") and §13.2 AS-34 Basis ("any value of 100 or less meets NIST") — the pack makes NIST SP 800-63B-4 [S76] its main authority for the sign-in limit and says the design "meets NIST". It leaves out that the same standard rejects a short PIN as a sole sign-in factor. That is counter-evidence from a source the pack already relies on, and the A criterion says it must be reported, not omitted — S76 §3.1.1 says: "A password (sometimes referred to as a passphrase or, if numeric, a personal identification number [PIN]) is a secret value…". §3.1.1.2 says verifiers "SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length", or 8 if they are only part of multi-factor sign-in. The card number identifies the member; it isn't a second factor. So a 4- or 6-digit library PIN falls short of NIST whatever the cap. "Meets NIST" also invites council IT, which validates AS-34, to read the sign-in as conforming to NIST. This is MINOR, not MAJOR, because what gets built doesn't change: card-and-PIN sign-in is the owner-approved default [A:Q-8], the LMS sets PINs, and the pack already puts a figure on the remaining risk (5–8%; RSK-15, High impact). I missed this in rounds 2 and 3, when I checked only §3.2.2. The PIN-length discussion added in v0.4 (AS-35, §9) makes it directly relevant now.
